Inspect attention and occlusion sensitivity

Where do predictions respond?

Attention shows the navigation transformer's weighting. Occlusion sensitivity measures how much the predicted trajectory changes when an image patch is masked.

FoveaNav snapshot at 0:07 in the robot-view clip. These maps are distinct from Gaussian gaze.

02 / RED-BAG FOLLOWING

Look beyond the target.

Gaze moves toward a nearby obstacle, then returns to the red bag. The surrounding scene remains available for trajectory prediction.

Why Gaussian gaze?

Focus attention. Retain context.

Gaze reweights attention over the full image. Peripheral information remains available.

01 / LOOK

Learn a gaze policy

Visual features and recent crop history guide where to look.

02 / WEIGHT

Apply Gaussian gaze

Temporally smoothed weights modulate cross-attention over all image tokens.

03 / MOVE

Predict a trajectory

BC trains trajectory prediction; RL learns gaze from trajectory error.

Why not a hard crop?

Following a target also requires avoiding obstacles.

With RL gaze learning in both variants, Gaussian conditioning succeeds more often than restricting navigation to a gaze-centered crop.

Red-Bag with obstacles, 10 trials per variant. Paper Table II; these are ablation results, not aggregate OOD success rates.

RL + Gaussian gaze 10 / 10
RL + hard crop 1 / 10

Learned from expert demonstrations, without human gaze annotations.

What information matters?

The target makes
the difference.

FoveaNav retains lower trajectory loss when corruption preserves the red bag. Its advantage narrows when corruption also affects the target.

Open-loop Red-Bag analysis. The 71% annotation is the reduction in the BC–FoveaNav loss gap, not a reduction in model loss.
